titulo.en: Sound of the day: the soft d

texto.en: Between two vowels, as in padre and madre, the Spanish d is soft: touch the tip of your tongue to the back of your upper teeth and let the air through, almost like the th in English “this”, but lighter. Say it slowly: padre, madre. (Abuelo and abuela have no d: the sound you hear there is a b.) At the beginning of a word, as in Daniela or don, the d is harder, closer to an English d.

titulo.en: Every noun has a gender: el / la, un / una

texto.en: In Spanish every noun is masculine or feminine, and the little word before it must match. For “the”, use el with a masculine noun and la with a feminine noun: el padre, la madre. For “a / an”, use un with a masculine noun and una with a feminine noun: un hermano, una hermana. Many masculine nouns end in -o and many feminine nouns end in -a: hermano and hermana, abuelo and abuela, hijo and hija. But this is only a tendency: padre is masculine and madre is feminine, and both end in -e. So learn each noun together with its article. In the plural, el becomes los, la becomes las, un becomes unos and una becomes unas: los hermanos, las hermanas. Careful: los hermanos can mean “the brothers” or “the brothers and sisters”. Also don't confuse el (the) with él (he): the accent mark changes the meaning.
The article follows the gender of the noun. Tap each phrase to hear it.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: r and rr

texto.en: The letter r is called “erre”. A single r inside a word, as in hermano, padre or profesor, is one quick tap of the tongue, like the tt in American English “butter”. The double rr, as in perro, and also an r at the beginning of a word, as in Rosa, is a trill: the tongue vibrates several times. Say them slowly: hermano, perros, profesores, Rosa. The difference matters: pero (but) and perro (dog) are different words.

To talk about more than one, nouns, articles and adjectives all take the plural, and they must agree: los profesores son ecuatorianos. If a word ends in a vowel, add -s: hermano becomes hermanos, ecuatoriano becomes ecuatorianos, estadounidense becomes estadounidenses. If it ends in a consonant, add -es: profesor becomes profesores, ciudad becomes ciudades. Watch the small changes: z changes to c (lápiz becomes lápices), a written accent mark can disappear (lección becomes lecciones, inglés becomes ingleses) or appear (joven becomes jóvenes) so the stress stays in the same place. The articles also change: el becomes los and la becomes las. A group with men and women, or a mixed group, uses the masculine plural: los estudiantes, los hermanos, los padres.
Tap each word to hear it. The last column gives the rule.

objetivo.en: Say how many siblings you have and how old they are, counting from 0 to 20.

nota.en: Irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen.
Plural: los años. The ñ sounds like the ny in “canyon”.
Literally “how many years do you have?”. Cuántos agrees with años.

explicacion.en: In Spanish you “have” years, you don't “are” them. Use tener for age: Tengo dieciocho años.
The yo form is irregular: tengo. The ie change only appears in tienes, tiene and tienen.
Cuántos has to agree with años (masculine plural): cuántos.

texto.en: In Spanish, two vowels together can make a single syllable, called a diphthong. The i (or u) is quick and light, like the y in “yes” or the w in “we”. Say tie-ne (“TYEH-neh”), tie-nen, nue-ve (“NWEH-veh”), vein-te (“VAYN-teh”), die-ci-sie-te. Keep it to one beat: tiene has two syllables, not three.

titulo.en: Tener: to have, and to be … years old

texto.en: Tener means “to have”. It is irregular: tengo (yo), tienes (tú), tiene (él, ella, usted), tenemos (nosotros, nosotras) and tienen (ustedes, ellos, ellas). Because the verb ending already shows who is speaking, you can drop the pronoun: Tengo un hermano. In Spanish you give your age with tener, not with ser: Tengo dieciocho años means “I am eighteen years old”, literally “I have eighteen years”. To ask, say ¿Cuántos años tienes? with tú, or ¿Cuántos años tiene? with usted. The numbers 0 to 20 are below. From 16 to 19 each number is a single word: dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve.
The pronoun can be dropped. Tap each form to hear it.
Tap each number to hear it.
Tap each number to hear it. The accent mark in dieciséis shows where the stress falls.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: the letter ñ

texto.en: The letter ñ (called “eñe”) is a separate letter in Spanish. It sounds like the ni in English “onion”, or the ny in “canyon”: the middle of your tongue touches the roof of your mouth. Say it slowly: compañera, señor, señora, año. Don't read it as a plain n: año has a ny sound in the middle, not an n.

titulo.en: Mi, tu, su, nuestro: my, your, his, her, our

texto.en: Possessives come before the noun and agree with the thing owned, not with the owner. Mi, tu and su have one form for masculine and feminine, and add -s for several things: mi hermano, mis hermanos; tu casa, tus casas; su perro, sus perros. Nuestro has four forms: nuestro perro, nuestra casa, nuestros perros, nuestras casas. Su means his, her, your (usted) or their, and the context tells you which one: sus padres can be Daniela's parents. Don't confuse tu (your) with tú (you): only the pronoun has an accent mark. Remember that Spanish does not use an apostrophe for possession: “Daniela's room” is el cuarto de Daniela.

titulo.en: What is this? There is a bed

objetivo.en: Say what there is in a place and ask and say what a nearby object is with este, esta and esto.

nota.en: Same form for one thing or several: hay una cama, hay dos sillas.
In gui the u is silent and the g is hard: “ghee-TAH-rrah”.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Es una cama en el cuarto.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Hay una cama en el cuarto.

explicacion.en: To say that something exists or is present in a place, use hay, not es. “There is a bed” is hay una cama.
Este and esta agree with the noun: libro is masculine, so este libro; mesa is feminine, so esta mesa.
When you don't know what the object is, use the neutral esto. Este and esta go with a noun you already know.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: qu and gu

texto.en: In que and qui, the u is silent: qu sounds like a plain k. Say qué (“keh”), aquí (“ah-KEE”), el queso, and not “kw”. In gue and gui, the u is silent too, and the g stays hard, like the g in “get”: la guitarra (“ghee-TAH-rrah”). But before a or o, the u is pronounced, like the w in “we”: agua (“AH-gwah”).

titulo.en: Hay, and this: este, esta, esto

texto.en: To say what there is in a place, use hay. It means both “there is” and “there are”, and it never changes: hay una cama, hay dos sillas. Don't use es for this: Hay una cama en el cuarto, not “Es una cama en el cuarto”. To say what something is, use es: Es una guitarra. To point at something near you, use este with a masculine noun and esta with a feminine noun: este libro, esta mesa. The word esto is neutral and is for something you can't name: ¿Qué es esto? Esto never goes with a noun. When the noun is already clear, este and esta can stand alone: Este es tu cuarto.
Choose by the gender of the noun. Tap each phrase to hear it.
